Superlatives  (Not Only but Also)
You use superlatives to talk about a noun with a highly developed quality. Not only but also, is used to mention a parallel or even an additional idea.
They're not only the brightest, but also the most accurate currently.
Colors will not only be the brightest, but they'll also be the most precise.

In order to form superlatives with short adjectives, you need to use the definite article the + adjective + suffix “est” + complement.

 

Example:

This is the brightest color in the palette.

 

With long adjectives (two or more syllables), you need to use the definite article the + most + adjective + complement.

 

Example:

We need to mix the most appealing colors together in the display.

 

On the other hand, you can use superlatives with the expression not only but also. It is useful when you need to emphasize more than one characteristic of someone or something. It’s used in two separate clauses. In the first clause, you use not only, and in the second one, you use but also. This last element is the one that provides an extra piece of information in the sentence. According to this, the structure will be as it follows:

Examples:

  • Computers provide not only the fastest, but also the most efficient tools to edit photos.
  • Good palettes show not only the biggest quantity of colors, but also the most realistic ones.
Simple Future
You can use the simple future to talk about a distant future, plans or things that you expect to happen.
But older devices will show mismatched colors.
Newer devices include a very capable CMS or color matching system that ensures that colors will look alike both in displays and prints.

In order to use the simple future, you need a subject, the auxiliary verb for the simple future "will", the main verb in base form and a complement.

 

Subject + will + main verb in base form + complement

 

Examples:

We will see more realistic colors in computer screens.

Displayed and printed colors will match better in newer systems.

 

Remember, after will, the verb goes without to, and it is not conjugated. In negative sentences, you can use "will not" or the contraction "won’t ".

 

Examples:

Displays won’t get larger in the future.

The display will not get larger in the future.

Diane: This print looks so bad. The colors are all washed out!
Lucy: They do. However, on the screen, they look far better. But I think it's because of the color space of both the computer and your printer.
Diane: What's that?
Lucy: Computer screens have evolved greatly. They're not only the brightest, but also the most accurate currently. Designers and users need colors to be displayed correctly. However, at first, they were monochrome or black and white. And then, they started to display more colors, though not at the same time, that's why you see palettes, which have only 266 colors to save on processing load. The same has happened with printers, they've become more accurate. But older devices will show mismatched colors.

Diane: Well, I need colors to be as accurate as possible.
Lucy: In that case, I recommend you update your devices. Colors will not only be the brightest, but they'll also be the most precise.
Diane: Why do I need to update my devices?
Lucy: The thing is that color in computing depends on many factors, for example, for color displays, they appear in the RGB system. Which refers to the three different colors of light that a screen can produce, red, green, and blue. So they mix and form the colors you see in the display in different intensities.

Diane: But what does that have to do with printing quality?
Lucy: A lot! Because in printing, there's a different color system which is CMYK, it stands for cyan, magenta, yellow, and black. They also mix in different intensities to form the colors the system requires. In older systems, colors didn't really match. Newer devices include a very capable CMS or color matching system that ensures that colors will look alike both in displays and prints.
